claims.text: Grip the bar underhand (palms up), hands about shoulder-width apart, so the wrists, elbows and shoulders line up.

quotes.text: Grip a bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands about shoulder-width apart.
Hold the barbell with both hands facing up so the wrists, elbows, and shoulders are in a straight line about shoulder-width apart.

claims.text: Stand with the feet about hip-width apart in a stable position, with good posture and the core braced for the whole lift.

quotes.text: Stand with your feet about hip-width apart and make sure that you’re standing in a stable position. Keep a good posture, and brace your core during the entire movement.

claims.text: Curl the bar toward the shoulders by bending the elbows, keeping them close to the body; the body stays still and only the arms move.

quotes.text: Lift the barbell toward the shoulders while bending the elbows and keeping them next to the middle of the body.
Curl up the barbell, and make sure that you keep your elbows close to your body the entire time. Your body shouldn’t move, just the arms.

claims.text: The upper arms must not travel back; keep them at the sides or let them move slightly forward.

quotes.text: Don’t let your upper arm travel back during the curl, keep it at your side or move it slightly forward.

claims.text: Elbows moving forward during the lift load the front delts instead of the biceps; elbows moving back let you cheat the weight up.

quotes.text: If your elbows move forward while you’re lifting the weight, it will put an additional load on your front delts, instead of focusing on your biceps. If your elbows move backward, you’ll also move the load from your biceps and be able to “cheat up” the weight.

claims.text: Too heavy a weight shows as swinging the body for momentum, or as half reps instead of the full range; the fix is less weight and a controlled lift.

quotes.text: By adding more weight than you can lift, you might start to swing your body and use momentum to get the weight up. Another sign of using too much weight is if you’re not using the full range of motion and start doing half reps instead.
quotes.where: Common mistakes, using too heavy weights

claims.text: If you start swinging the bar with body momentum, take weight off and lift with control.

quotes.text: If you start to swing to move the barbell with help from the momentum of the body, you should probably remove some weight instead and focus on performing the movement with control.
Trunk movements together with knee flexions were visually monitored by the researchers to avoid possible cheating.

claims.text: Keep the wrists straight during the lift; bent wrists put extra load on them and can lead to discomfort.

quotes.text: Keep your wrists straight during the movement. If they’re bent, it can put an unnecessary load on them and lead to discomfort and maybe even injuries.
quotes.where: Common mistakes, not locking your wrists

claims.text: Lower the bar slowly back to the start, keeping the chest still.

quotes.text: Slowly lower the weight to return to the starting position. Keep chest still, using just the arms for the movement.

claims.text: Keep tension in the muscles at the bottom and do not let the elbows travel backward.

quotes.text: To accomplish this, avoid letting your elbows travel backward during the lift, and also keep tension in the muscles in the bottom position.

claims.text: Compared with dumbbells, the barbell usually allows heavier weights but gives less range of motion and less freedom at the wrists.

quotes.text: Barbell curls often allow for heavier weights to be lifted, but they offer less range of motion and flexibility in your wrists.

claims.text: Muscles: the barbell curl mainly works the biceps and brachialis, with the forearm flexors as secondary. In an EMG study the straight-bar curl activated the biceps and brachioradialis at least as much as the dumbbell curl, close to the EZ-bar curl.

quotes.text: The barbell curl primarily targets your biceps and brachialis (which lie beneath the biceps), but the forearm flexors are also involved as a secondary muscle group.

the DC variant was found to be less effective, while the BC variant could be placed in an intermediate position but with an activation closer to the EZ than to the DC variant for the two muscles investigated.

claims.text: Tempo (up = lifting, down = lowering): a study protocol used 3 s per full repetition; ACSM advises moderate speed (1-2 s up, 1-2 s down).

quotes.text: The metronome was set so that each repetition duration was 3 s.
at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

plate.viewWhy: Elbow bend, upper arms travelling back or forward (c4, c5) and body swing (c7) read side-on; the bar is seen end-on. Census view is side.
plate.equipment: Barbell held at the thighs, standing on the floor line (census: barbell hangs at the thighs).
plate.start: Standing, feet hip-width, core braced (c2); arms hanging straight, bar at the thighs, palms forward, hands shoulder-width (c1); wrists straight (c8).
plate.end: Elbows bent, bar near the shoulders (c3); upper arms at the sides or slightly forward, never back (c4); chest and body still (c9, c3).

checkpoints.what: Upper arms stay by the body and never travel back.

checkpoints.label: Straight wrists
checkpoints.what: Hands in line with the forearms, not bent up or down.

mistake.what: Swinging: leaning back and using the hips and knees to throw the bar up.
mistake.why: StrengthLog names swinging as the sign of too much weight (c6, c7); an EMG study watched trunk and knee movement as cheating (c7).
mistake.rankNote: StrengthLog lists elbow position, too much weight and bent wrists without ranking them; swinging is drawn as on the parent card, and elbows travelling back (c5) is the layer’s second picture.

grip.type: Underhand (palms up), full grip on a straight bar.
grip.width: About shoulder-width, wrists, elbows and shoulders in a line (c1).
grip.wrist: Straight, in line with the forearm; the straight bar gives the wrists less freedom than dumbbells (c11).

Grip the bar underhand, hands shoulder-width.
Let the arms hang straight with the bar at your thighs.

Use the full range, not half reps.
